Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Places of worship or religious gatherings

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette:
Keilani has always felt most at home under an open sky, which made her work as a park ranger a natural fit. For fifteen years, the steady rhythm of the seasons and the quiet grandeur of the wilderness were her sanctuary. But that was before her six-month leave to volunteer with a relief agency. Now, the familiar trails feel alien, bordered by unseen threats. She spends her days at the visitor center scanning faces, not with the welcoming gaze of a ranger, but with the sharp, assessing eye of a sentry. She is certain that danger can wear any face, and she watches constantly for the one that will betray a hidden intent. Any tourist making a sudden gesture for a camera or map causes an immediate, full-body clench, a spike of adrenaline that leaves her trembling and breathless. Her world, once expansive, has shrunk to the park and her home; she refuses to go anywhere new, believing that only in familiar territory can she possibly anticipate the dangers that await.

The event that broke her world is not a story she can tell. When she tries, even in the privacy of her own mind, the narrative shatters. There are fragments, some so vivid they feel like they are happening right now: the cloying, sweet smell of the local commander’s cologne, a mix of jasmine and sandalwood, as he leaned in to thank her. The rough texture of his jacket as he pulled her into a brief, firm hug, a gesture of solidarity. She remembers his smile. Then, there is a gap, a silent, black void where the next few minutes should be. The memory picks up again with a searing flash of light, the roar of an explosion that she felt in her bones, and the taste of dust and blood. The moments between the hug and the blast are simply gone, and this blankness terrifies her. Trying to explain it to her husband, Mark, is impossible; she starts, finds herself lost in the vividness of the scent or the smile, and then the thread is gone, leaving her staring into space, unable to finish.

In the year since her return, these fragments have ambushed her without warning. A whiff of a similar cologne on a hiker sent her scrambling off-trail, gasping for air. More painfully, any attempt at physical affection has become a source of terror. When Mark, trying to comfort her after a nightmare, reaches to hold her, her body reacts before her mind can. She flinches away, seeing not her husband of ten years but the smiling commander, the hug no longer a gesture of peace but a signal of imminent betrayal and death. This reaction has carved a chasm between them. He has stopped trying to touch her, and the silence in their home feels as vast and empty as the blank space in her memory. She feels she no longer belongs with him, or anywhere. The person she was—compassionate, trusting, brave—seems to have died in that clinic. She is haunted by the belief that her trust was a fatal mistake, that by believing the commander, she had a hand in what happened, violating her most fundamental value to protect others.

This sense of alienation has bled into every corner of her life. She and Mark used to be active in their local church, but she can no longer set foot inside. The quiet reverence feels like a lie, a mockery of the violent chaos she knows the world contains. She avoids doctors, too; a deep gash on her leg from a fallen branch was clumsily stitched at her own kitchen table because the thought of being in a clinical setting, of surrendering control to a professional, was unbearable. It was Mark who finally gave her an ultimatum, his voice gentle but firm, telling her he was watching her disappear. She is here now not out of hope, but out of a weary sense of obligation, and a deeper, more terrifying feeling that has taken root in the quiet hours of the night: a growing certainty that her life is no longer worth living.
